nameStory: The Eastern Small-footed Myotis gets its name from its remarkably tiny feet - among the smallest of any bat in eastern North America! The word 'myotis' comes from Greek meaning 'mouse ear,' referring to the shape of their ears that reminded early naturalists of tiny mouse ears.
description: This is one of New England's smallest and rarest bats, a tiny winged mammal that you're unlikely to encounter but incredibly lucky if you do. With only 16 recorded observations across all of New England, spotting one is like finding a needle in a haystack. These diminutive bats are distinguished by their distinctive black face mask that makes them look like tiny flying bandits. They belong to the mouse-eared bat family and hibernate in hard-to-reach rocky crevices rather than the caves where most other bats gather.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Extremely small bat with disproportionately tiny feet that feel delicate as twigs if handled by researchers - among the smallest bat feet in eastern North America

idTips.label: Face
idTips.description: Distinctive black mask across the face and ears, making it look like a miniature superhero - this dark facial coloring is unique among New England bats

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Golden-brown to yellowish fur that feels soft and dense, contrasting sharply with the dark face mask

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Rarely seen in traditional winter bat surveys because they hibernate alone in tiny rock crevices rather than clustering in caves with other bats

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in mountainous rocky areas where they can squeeze into impossibly narrow cliff face cracks and stone crevices

habitat: Seeks out mountainous and rocky terrain throughout New England's higher elevations, particularly areas with exposed cliff faces and stone outcroppings. They favor regions where they can access tiny crevices in rocks for roosting and hibernation. Unlike other bats that gather in caves, these solitary creatures prefer the isolation of narrow rock fissures.

seasonality.spring: Emerges from winter hibernation in rocky crevices and becomes active hunting insects, though sightings remain extremely rare.
seasonality.summer: Active period for hunting and raising young, but still incredibly elusive and unlikely to be observed during typical evening bat-watching.
seasonality.fall: Preparing for hibernation by feeding heavily on insects before retreating to rocky winter roosts.
seasonality.winter: Hibernating alone in narrow rock crevices, making them nearly impossible to find during winter bat surveys that focus on caves.

funFact: These bats are so good at hiding that most of the 16 New England sightings have happened only in the past couple decades - they were likely here all along, just masters of staying invisible in their rocky hideouts!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Little Brown Bats, but the Eastern Small-footed Myotis has that distinctive black face mask that looks like it's wearing a bandit's disguise - no other New England bat sports this dramatic facial coloring.
contextualKnowledge: Until recently, all small-footed bats in North America were thought to be the same species, but scientists discovered that western populations are actually a completely different species. This means our eastern version is even more special and geographically limited than previously understood.
compareHints: Compared to its mouse-eared bat cousins like the Little Brown Bat and Northern Myotis, the Eastern Small-footed Myotis is noticeably smaller with that unmistakable black face mask. While Little Brown Bats and others hibernate in large groups in caves, this species goes it alone in rocky crevices. Its feet are also proportionally much smaller than other Myotis species, making it unique even when examined up close.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the mouse-eared bats in New England, the little brown bat has the glossiest, most reflective fur compared to the Northern Myotis which appears more matte and grayish-brown.

Among New England's mouse-eared bats, the Northern Myotis stands out with its distinctively long ears - much longer than the Little Brown Bat's modest rounded ears or the Indiana Bat's medium-length ears.
Among the mouse-eared bats, Indiana bats are most similar to Little Brown Bats but have smaller feet with less toe hair and distinctive pink lips.
